lessons.title: Strings and Time
lessons.explanation:
# 04 · Strings and Time

Two topics, one theme: **both look simple and both have a hidden parameter
you did not set.** For strings it is the culture. For dates it is the clock
and the timezone. Nearly every bug in this module is invisible on your
machine and appears on a server configured differently — which is the worst
kind, because the test suite is green.

## The mental model

### 1 · A string never changes

```csharp
var s = "a";
s += "b";      // a NEW string; the old one is garbage
```

For two or three pieces that is irrelevant. In a loop it copies roughly
n² characters. Reach for `string.Join` first (it solves the
separator-between-items problem, so there is no trailing comma to trim) and
`StringBuilder` when `Join` cannot express the shape.

### 2 · Formatting has two audiences

| audience | wants | use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a machine (CSV, JSON, a log, another service) | stable, culture-free, round-trippable | `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` |
| a human | their own separators and symbols | a specific `CultureInfo` |

The bug is using the *ambient* culture for the machine case. Your export
writes `1.234,50` on a German server and the importer that wrote it cannot
read it back.

```csharp
amount.ToString(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)   // "1234.5" everywhere
decimal.TryParse(text, NumberStyles.Number, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, out var v)
```

Note `decimal` keeps its **scale**: `0.10m` formats as `"0.10"`, because the
value remembers how precise it was. `double` cannot do that.

### 3 · A regex matches anywhere unless you anchor it

```csharp
Regex.IsMatch("xAB-1234junk", @"[A-Z]{2}-\d{4}")     // true  — probably a bug
Regex.IsMatch("xAB-1234junk", @"^[A-Z]{2}-\d{4}$")   // false — validation
```

Every validation pattern needs `^` and `$`. In .NET `$` also matches before
a trailing newline; `\z` is the strict end.

### 4 · Pick the type that matches the concept

| concept | type | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a birthday, a check-in date, an invoice date | `DateOnly` | no time to be shifted across midnight |
| a time of day with no date | `TimeOnly` | opening hours, alarms |
| a moment that happened | `DateTimeOffset` (UTC) | unambiguous, comparable |
| a duration | `TimeSpan` | not a date at all |
| `DateTime` | — | carries a `Kind` flag that is silently wrong more often than right |

### 5 · Time is a dependency

```csharp
bool IsExpired(DateTimeOffset issued, TimeSpan ttl, IClock clock) =>
    clock.Now >= issued + ttl;
```

A method that reads `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow` internally has an input you
cannot set, so its boundary cases can only be tested by waiting — which is
why those are the cases that break. Pass the clock. (.NET 8 ships
`TimeProvider` for this; a one-property `IClock` is the same idea.)

## The details that bite

1. **`ToLower()` and `ToUpper()` use the current culture.** For keys, ids
   and protocol tokens use `ToLowerInvariant` or, better,
   `StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase` on the comparison itself.
2. **An unanchored validation regex accepts anything with your pattern
   somewhere inside it.**
3. **Constructing a `Regex` parses it.** Doing that per request repeats the
   work forever. Hoist it into a `static readonly` field, or use the static
   `Regex.IsMatch` helpers (they keep a small cache), or `[GeneratedRegex]`.
4. **Nested quantifiers backtrack catastrophically.** `(\s*\w+)+` on a
   30-character near-match can pin a core. Keep validation patterns boring
   and cap the input length.
5. **`TimeSpan.Hours` is the component (0–23); `TotalHours` is the whole
   span.** A 26-hour span has `Hours == 2`.
6. **Date subtraction through `DateTime` drags in hours**, which can be 23
   or 25 long when a clock changes. `DateOnly.DayNumber` differences cannot.
7. **`AddYears` clamps 29 February to the 28th** in a common year rather
   than throwing — a decision the library makes for you.
8. **Ages are not `(now - born).Days / 365`.** Compute the anniversary and
   check whether it has passed.

## Exercises

| # | file | ★ | what you build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `01-building-strings.cs` | ★☆☆ | `Join` over `+=`, a CSV field that needs quoting, indenting a block |
| 02 | `02-formatting-and-parsing.cs` | ★★☆ | one format for machines, one for humans, and a parse that cannot throw |
| 03 | `03-regex-basics.cs` | ★★☆ | anchors, a match-all, and a masking replace |
| 04 | `04-dates-without-tears.cs` | ★★☆ | business days, nights between, and the age bug |
| 05 | `05-durations-and-the-clock.cs` | ★★☆ | expiry you can test, humanised spans, capped backoff |

```
dotnet run exercises/04-dates-without-tears.cs
dotnet run solutions/04-dates-without-tears.cs
dotnet run ../verify.cs 04
dotnet run ../progress.cs 04
```

---

**Stuck?** `cheatsheets/csharp-language.md` (strings, formatting, regex, time) · **Self-check:** `quizzes/04-strings-and-time.md` · **Next:** `bootcamp/05-types-and-oop`

unit.title: Text in, text out, and the culture in between
Patterns that match what you meant
Durations, and a clock you can control

csbootcamp/04-strings-and-time/01-buildi.instructions:
**Concepts:** immutability · StringBuilder · string.Join  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

Strings are immutable, so every += builds a whole new one. Three
small builders, each with a rule that makes concatenation in a loop
the wrong tool:

    Csv(["a", "b,c"])          → a,"b,c"     (quote a field with a comma)
    Repeat("ab", 3, "-")       → ab-ab-ab
    Indent("x\ny", 2)          → "  x\n  y"  (every line, blank ones too)

Indent must use "\n" as the line separator so the tests behave the
same on every machine.

hint: string.Join handles the separator-between-items problem for
you — no trailing separator to trim. StringBuilder is for the cases
Join cannot express, and Split(char) plus Join is often shorter than
either.
csbootcamp/04-strings-and-time/01-buildi.explanation:
A string never changes. `s += x` allocates a new string and copies
both halves, so building n pieces in a loop copies roughly n squared
characters and leaves n dead strings for the collector. For two or
three pieces that is irrelevant; inside a loop it is the classic
performance bug, and StringBuilder (a growable buffer, one final
allocation) is the answer.
But before StringBuilder, try string.Join. It solves the problem
everyone gets wrong by hand — the separator goes BETWEEN items, so
there is no trailing comma to trim and no "is this the first
iteration?" flag. All three methods here fall out of Join plus a
projection, which is why none of them needs a builder.
Csv shows the projection carrying a rule: quote only the fields that
need it. Real CSV also escapes embedded quotes and handles newlines —
this is a teaching-sized version, and the honest advice is to use a
real CSV library the moment the data is not yours.
Indent splits, maps, and rejoins. Splitting on '\n' and rejoining
with '\n' round-trips exactly, including blank lines, which is why
the blank-line test passes without a special case.
One more tool worth knowing: raw string literals (three quotes) for
multi-line text with no escaping, and interpolation with alignment
and format specifiers for tables.

csbootcamp/04-strings-and-time/02-format.instructions:
**Concepts:** format strings · InvariantCulture · TryParse  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

The same number is "1234.5" to a machine, "1,234.50" to a British
reader and "1.234,50" to a German one. Which one you produce is a
choice, and not making it is how a CSV export becomes unreadable by
the importer that wrote it.

    ForMachines(1234.5m)        → "1234.5"     (invariant, round-trip)
    ForHumans(1234.5m)          → "1,234.50"   (en-GB, two decimals)
    ParseAmount("1234.5")       → 1234.5m
    ParseAmount("nonsense")     → null
    Pad("ab", 5)                → "ab   "      (left-aligned, width 5)

ParseAmount must accept machine format regardless of the machine's
own culture, and must never throw.

hint: every ToString and Parse has an IFormatProvider overload.
CultureInfo.InvariantCulture is the one that never changes.
decimal.TryParse takes NumberStyles and a culture.
csbootcamp/04-strings-and-time/02-format.explanation:
There are exactly two audiences for formatted text and they want
opposite things. A MACHINE wants a stable, culture-free shape it can
read back — CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, no grouping separators, and
ideally a round-trip format. A HUMAN wants their own conventions —
a specific CultureInfo, grouping, currency symbols, local date order.
The bug is using the ambient culture for the machine case: the export
runs on a German server, writes "1.234,50", and the importer reads
1.23450 or throws. It passes every test in London.
ForMachines just calls ToString with the invariant culture: a
decimal's default format already round-trips and PRESERVES its scale,
so 0.10m prints as "0.10" and 1234.5m as "1234.5". A custom format
string like "0.0#" would drop that trailing zero — decimal remembers
how precise the value was, and double never could.
ParseAmount pins the culture too, and uses TryParse so bad input is a
value (null) rather than an exception. Returning decimal? makes the
failure part of the type: the caller cannot forget to handle it,
which an exception lets them do by default.
NumberStyles.Number allows a leading sign, decimal point and
whitespace but not currency symbols or exponents — narrow it further
if the input is meant to be strict.
Pad shows the third spelling: PadRight, or an alignment in an
interpolated string. Both stop at the width you asked for and neither
truncates, which is why the long-value test passes untouched.

csbootcamp/04-strings-and-time/03-regex-.instructions:
**Concepts:** Regex · anchors · character classes · Replace  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Three jobs a regex is genuinely the right tool for:

    IsReference("AB-1234")     → true
    IsReference("xAB-1234")    → false   (anchored: the WHOLE string)
    Hashtags("hi #a and #b!")  → ["#a", "#b"]
    MaskDigits("card 4111111111111111 ok")
                               → "card **** ok"

A reference is exactly two uppercase letters, a hyphen, and four
digits. MaskDigits replaces any run of 12 or more digits with four
asterisks and leaves shorter numbers alone.

hint: without anchors a regex matches ANYWHERE in the string, which
is the single most common regex bug in validation code. Use a
compiled static readonly Regex for anything used more than once, and
remember that + is greedy — it takes as much as it can.
csbootcamp/04-strings-and-time/03-regex-.explanation:
Anchors are the whole lesson of IsReference. Regex.IsMatch asks "does
this pattern occur ANYWHERE in the input", so an unanchored
validation regex happily accepts "xAB-1234junk". Wrapping the pattern
in ^ and $ makes it "the entire string is this shape". Every
validator you write needs them, and forgetting them is the bug that
lets an attacker append anything they like to a value you checked.
(In .NET, $ also matches before a trailing newline — for input that
might carry one, backslash-z is the strict end-of-string anchor.)
Where the pattern LIVES matters. Constructing a Regex parses and
compiles it, so `new Regex(...)` inside a per-request method repeats
that work forever. The static Regex.IsMatch/Matches/Replace methods
used here keep a small internal cache, which is why they are fine for
a handful of patterns. In a real class you would hoist them into
`static readonly Regex` fields (top-level statements cannot declare
those — a file-based app has locals, not fields), and add
RegexOptions.Compiled for a genuinely hot one. .NET 7+ also has the
[GeneratedRegex] source generator, which builds the matcher at
compile time with no startup cost at all.
Hashtags uses Matches, which returns every non-overlapping match, and
a character class that says where a tag ENDS: word characters only,
so the comma and the space stop it. Being explicit about the ending
is usually easier than being clever about the beginning.
MaskDigits shows Replace with a quantifier range: {12,} is "twelve or
more", and + being greedy means a long run is replaced once rather
than in pieces. Test the boundary — 11 digits must survive — because
a quantifier off by one is invisible until real data arrives.
And the standing warning: a nested quantifier over an ambiguous group
can backtrack catastrophically. Keep validation patterns boring, and
cap input length before matching.

csbootcamp/04-strings-and-time/04-dates-.instructions:
**Concepts:** DateOnly · date arithmetic · the age bug  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A calendar date is not a moment in time, and using DateTime for one
is how bookings move by a day when the server changes timezone.
DateOnly exists for exactly this. Three calculations:

    NextBusinessDay(Fri 2026-03-06) → Mon 2026-03-09
    NightsBetween(03-01, 03-04)     → 3
    AgeOn(born 2000-06-15, on 2026-06-14) → 25   (birthday not yet)
    AgeOn(born 2000-06-15, on 2026-06-15) → 26   (birthday today)

NextBusinessDay always moves forward at least one day and never
lands on a Saturday or Sunday.

hint: DateOnly has AddDays and DayOfWeek. The gap between two dates
is (a.DayNumber - b.DayNumber). For the age, compare the month and
day AFTER subtracting the years — that comparison is the exercise.
csbootcamp/04-strings-and-time/04-dates-.explanation:
Use the type that matches the concept. A birthday, a check-in date
and an invoice date are CALENDAR dates: no time, no zone, no
midnight to be pushed across by a UTC conversion. DateOnly says that
in the type system. A moment in time — when a row was written, when a
token expires — is a DateTimeOffset, stored in UTC. Plain DateTime
sits awkwardly between the two and carries a Kind flag that is
silently wrong more often than it is right.
NextBusinessDay steps once and then keeps stepping while it is on a
weekend. Writing it as "add 1, then skip" rather than a table of
special cases means Friday, Saturday and Sunday all fall out of the
same two lines.
NightsBetween uses DayNumber, the count of days since year 1. It is
the honest way to subtract dates: no TimeSpan, no hours, nothing that
can be 23 or 25 long because a clock changed.
AgeOn is the classic. Subtracting the years gives the answer only if
the birthday has already happened this year — so compute the
anniversary in the target year and take one off when the date has not
reached it. The leap-day test is why AddYears is the right tool
rather than constructing a new date by hand: AddYears CLAMPS 29
February to 28 February in a common year instead of throwing, which
decides — for you — that a leap-day birthday falls on the 28th. That
is a defensible convention and it is also a product decision; if your
domain says 1 March, you have to write that yourself. The point is
that the library made a choice and you should know which one.
The general rule: any date calculation that mentions "today" should
take the date as a PARAMETER. A method that reads DateTime.Now
internally cannot be tested at a boundary, which is exactly where its
bugs live. The next exercise makes that injection explicit.

csbootcamp/04-strings-and-time/05-durati.instructions:
**Concepts:** TimeSpan · injected time · testable expiry  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Code that calls DateTimeOffset.UtcNow directly cannot be tested at
its boundaries — you would have to wait. Take the clock as a
parameter instead. IClock and a FixedClock for tests are at the
BOTTOM of this file.

    IsExpired(issued, ttl: 5m, clock at issued + 4m59s) → false
    IsExpired(issued, ttl: 5m, clock at issued + 5m)    → true
    Humanize(2h 5m)      → "2h 5m"
    Humanize(45s)        → "45s"
    Backoff(0)           → 1s      (then 2s, 4s, 8s…, capped at 30s)

Expiry is inclusive: exactly at the deadline counts as expired.

hint: TimeSpan.FromSeconds and the arithmetic operators do the work.
For the backoff, doubling is a left shift or Math.Pow — mind the cap
BEFORE the number gets huge, because attempt 40 overflows.
csbootcamp/04-strings-and-time/05-durati.explanation:
The design lesson comes first: time is a DEPENDENCY. A method that
reads DateTimeOffset.UtcNow has a hidden input you cannot set, so its
boundary cases — one second before expiry, exactly at expiry — can
only be tested by waiting, which nobody does, which is why those are
the cases that break. One interface with one property removes the
problem entirely, and the tests here run in microseconds because of
it. (.NET 8 ships TimeProvider for exactly this; a hand-rolled IClock
is the same idea and works everywhere.)
IsExpired is then one comparison, and the >= is the whole
specification: "exactly at the deadline counts as expired" is a
decision, and writing it as >= rather than > is where it gets
recorded. Off-by-one in time is the same bug class as off-by-one in
an index.
Humanize is a switch on magnitude, largest unit first. TimeSpan
exposes both Hours (the hour COMPONENT, 0-23) and TotalHours (the
whole span as a fraction) and mixing them up is the standard bug —
a 26-hour span has Hours == 2. Here the components are what we want
because the largest unit is chosen explicitly.
Backoff caps by taking the MINIMUM of the doubled value and the
ceiling, and it does the doubling in a way that cannot overflow: cap
the exponent first. `1 << 1000` is undefined-ish nonsense and
Math.Pow(2, 1000) is Infinity, which converts to a TimeSpan that
throws. Guarding the input rather than the output is the habit.
